# Treaties, diplomacy and international law (`international_law_sovereignty`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by alphabet_writing, postal_system, balance_of_power
- Core idea: States treat each other as equals that keep written treaties, do not harm envoys, and accept common rules for war, trade and the sea even without a ruler above them. It works through reciprocity and reputation: a state that kills ambassadors or breaks treaties finds nobody will deal with it. The tools are permanent resident ambassadors with immunity, treaties in agreed duplicate texts, arbitration by a third party, safe-conducts for merchants, and the principle that each ruler is master in his own territory and may not be attacked over his religion.
- Pitfalls:
  - Expecting enforcement: there is no court with an army; rules hold where breaking them costs reputation or invites a coalition
  - Repeating the story that the Peace of Westphalia (1648) founded sovereign equality: the treaties say little of the kind, and the idea is a later reading
  - Thinking diplomacy and treaties are modern or European: the Amarna letters, the Egyptian-Hittite treaty, Chinese interstate covenants and Islamic siyar are all older
  - Sending envoys without credentials, gifts and knowledge of protocol: in most eras a breach of form is an insult and can cost the envoy's life
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2350 BC – treaty between Ebla and Abarsal, the oldest surviving treaty text; c. 2450 BC Lagash-Umma border settlement on the Stele of the Vultures; egypt: c. 1350 BC – Amarna letters: Egypt, Babylon, Mitanni, Hatti and Assyria correspond as 'brothers' in Akkadian; c. 1259 BC Egyptian-Hittite peace treaty after Kadesh, surviving in both versions; china: 7th–5th c. BC – sworn covenants (meng) among the Spring and Autumn states; 546 BC peace conference at Song; india: c. 3rd c. BC–3rd c. AD – Arthashastra: circle of states, six policies, inviolability of envoys; greece: 5th–4th c. BC – heralds, proxenoi (resident representatives), interstate arbitration, common peace treaties; rome: Republic – fetial rites for declaring just war; ius gentium as law common to all peoples; islamic: c. 800 – al-Shaybani's Siyar, a systematic law of war, treaties and safe-conduct (aman) for foreigners; europe: c. 1450s – permanent resident ambassadors among the Italian states after the Peace of Lodi (1454); 1625 Grotius; 1648 Peace of Westphalia; 1815 Congress of Vienna fixes diplomatic ranks; americas: wampum belts record treaties among and with the Haudenosaunee (17th–18th c.)
- Read:
  - Hugo Grotius, De jure belli ac pacis (1625)
  - Garrett Mattingly, Renaissance Diplomacy (1955)
  - Mario Liverani, International Relations in the Ancient Near East, 1600–1100 BC (2001)
